requirements: Caller must hold the allocator lock at least in reader mode.
obj_base must be the real base address of a GC object (debug header address if debug-allocated).

functions.name: GC_push_all
functions.description: Pushes everything in the memory range [bottom, top) onto the mark stack for later scanning.
requirements: bottom and top define a valid address range with bottom <= top.
Should only be used when there is no possibility of mark stack overflow.

functions.name: GC_push_all_eager
functions.description: Pushes and immediately scans references in the range [bottom, top), treating interior pointers as valid. Intended for ranges whose contents may change.
requirements: bottom and top define a valid address range with bottom <= top.

functions.name: GC_push_conditional
functions.description: Pushes references in [bottom, top) either for all pages or only dirty pages depending on the all flag.
requirements: bottom and top define a valid address range with bottom <= top.
all must be either 0 (process only dirty pages) or non-zero (process all pages).

functions.name: GC_push_finalizer_structures
functions.description: Pushes the collector’s internal finalizer-related structures as roots during marking.
requirements: Intended for internal/advanced use during marking; caller should ensure appropriate collector state if calling directly.

functions.name: GC_set_push_other_roots
functions.description: Sets the client hook used to push additional non-standard roots. A client-supplied procedure should also call the previously registered one.
requirements: proc may be null to clear the hook.
Both setter and getter require external synchronization to avoid data races with concurrent updates/reads.
Client hook should chain to the original/previous hook.

functions.name: GC_get_push_other_roots
functions.description: Gets the currently registered push-other-roots hook.
requirements: External synchronization is required to avoid data races with concurrent updates.

functions.name: GC_enumerate_reachable_objects_inner
functions.description: Walks the GC heap and invokes cb for each reachable object, passing object base and size. The allocator lock must be held by the caller; the callback runs under the same lock mode.
requirements: cb must be non-null.
Caller must hold the allocator lock at least in reader mode for the duration of the enumeration and callback calls.

functions.name: GC_is_tmp_root
functions.description: Returns non-zero if the given address lies within the collector’s temporary static root sections. For debugging only.
requirements: Function acquires the allocator lock in reader mode internally; no external synchronization required for the query.
addr is any address to test.

functions.name: GC_print_trace
functions.description: Prints tracing information for the specified GC cycle number. Public wrapper variant.
requirements: gc_no identifies the GC cycle to print trace for; valid range depends on collector history.
May acquire internal synchronization as needed by the implementation.

functions.name: GC_print_trace_inner
functions.description: Inner variant of GC_print_trace that follows the library’s “_inner” pattern; intended to be called with the allocator lock held.
requirements: Caller should hold the allocator lock when invoking this inner variant.
gc_no identifies the GC cycle to print trace for.

functions.name: GC_set_on_mark_stack_empty
functions.description: Sets a callback invoked when the mark stack becomes empty; the callback can push additional work (e.g., to implement ephemerons). Setter acquires the allocator lock.
requirements: cb may be null to clear the callback.
Setter acquires the allocator lock; no extra synchronization needed to set.
The callback must accept and return the mark stack pointers it updates appropriately.

functions.name: GC_get_on_mark_stack_empty
functions.description: Gets the currently registered on-mark-stack-empty callback. Getter acquires the allocator lock in reader mode.
requirements: None beyond standard call semantics; the getter acquires the allocator lock (reader mode).

functions.name: GC_make_descriptor
functions.signature: GC_descr GC_make_descriptor(const GC_word* bm, size_t number_of_bits_in_bitmap);
functions.description: Constructs a typed allocation descriptor from a bitmap describing which pointer-sized words in an object may contain pointers. The bitmap least-significant bit corresponds to the first pointer-sized word in the object. number_of_bits_in_bitmap is the count of meaningful bits in bm (typically the object size measured in pointer-sized words). Intended to be created once per type and reused for allocations; building descriptors may consume a finite internal resource. If memory is insufficient to build the precise descriptor, a conservative approximation is returned.
requirements: bm must reference at least ceil(number_of_bits_in_bitmap / GC_WORDSZ) GC_word elements (i.e., enough words to cover the meaningful bits in the bitmap).

number_of_bits_in_bitmap should match the number of pointer-sized words that may contain pointers in the intended object layout; extra object words beyond this count are assumed to contain no pointers.
On targets noted in the header (e.g., cris, m68k; and some compilers), all pointer fields in the described type must be aligned to pointer size.
Callers should create a descriptor once per type (not per allocation) to avoid exhausting the finite internal resource.

functions.name: GC_malloc_explicitly_typed
functions.description: Allocates a zeroed object whose layout is described by descriptor d. This object is managed by the collector using the provided explicit type information rather than conservative scanning. The object must not be resized with GC_realloc or GC_reallocf.
requirements: size_in_bytes must be at least (number_of_bits_in_bitmap in d) * sizeof(void*); allocating smaller than the descriptor’s meaningful bits is not allowed.

d must be a descriptor produced for the object’s layout (typically via GC_make_descriptor) and must correctly describe which pointer-sized words in the first (number_of_bits_in_bitmap) words may contain pointers.
The returned object is cleared to zero.
Do not pass the returned object to GC_realloc() or GC_reallocf().
On targets noted in the header (e.g., cris, m68k), pointer fields in the described type must be pointer-size aligned.

functions.name: GC_malloc_explicitly_typed_ignore_off_page
functions.description: Allocates a zeroed object like GC_malloc_explicitly_typed but using the collector’s ignore-off-page allocation variant. This affects internal collector treatment of pointers to the object (e.g., off-page pointers); caller-facing usage is otherwise the same.
requirements: size_in_bytes must be at least (number_of_bits_in_bitmap in d) * sizeof(void*).
d must be a valid descriptor for the object’s layout (e.g., from GC_make_descriptor).
The returned object is cleared to zero.
Do not pass the returned object to GC_realloc() or GC_reallocf().
On targets noted in the header (e.g., cris, m68k), pointer fields in the described type must be pointer-size aligned.

functions.name: GC_calloc_explicitly_typed
functions.signature: void* GC_calloc_explicitly_typed(size_t nelements, size_t element_size_in_bytes, GC_descr d);
functions.description: Allocates and clears an array of nelements elements, each of element_size_in_bytes, where each element’s layout is described by descriptor d. Uses explicit type information to guide the collector.
requirements: element_size_in_bytes must be a multiple of the platform’s pointer alignment requirement (e.g., on a 32-bit machine with 16-bit pointer alignment, element_size_in_bytes must be a multiple of 2).
element_size_in_bytes must be at least (number_of_bits_in_bitmap in d) * sizeof(void*).
d must describe the element layout; the same descriptor is applied per element.
The returned array is cleared to zero.
On targets noted in the header (e.g., cris, m68k), pointer fields in the described type must be pointer-size aligned.

functions.name: GC_calloc_prepare_explicitly_typed
functions.signature: int GC_calloc_prepare_explicitly_typed(struct GC_calloc_typed_descr_s* p_ctd, size_t sizeof_ctd, size_t nelements, size_t element_size_in_bytes, GC_descr d);
functions.description: Prepares an internal description for efficiently allocating one or more typed arrays having the same element layout (d) and nelements/element_size_in_bytes. The preparation result is stored in *p_ctd even on failure. Returns 1 on success, 0 on failure. Call GC_calloc_do_explicitly_typed with the prepared descriptor to perform the allocations.
requirements: p_ctd must point to writable storage for a struct GC_calloc_typed_descr_s.
sizeof_ctd must equal sizeof(struct GC_calloc_typed_descr_s).
nelements and element_size_in_bytes define the array shape that will be used later with GC_calloc_do_explicitly_typed; subsequent allocations using this prepared descriptor must match these values.
element_size_in_bytes must be a multiple of the platform’s pointer alignment requirement (same constraint as GC_calloc_explicitly_typed).
element_size_in_bytes must be at least (number_of_bits_in_bitmap in d) * sizeof(void*).
d must correctly describe the element layout.
The caller may ignore the return value, since the prepared result is stored in *p_ctd and will be checked by GC_calloc_do_explicitly_typed().

functions.name: GC_calloc_do_explicitly_typed
functions.signature: void* GC_calloc_do_explicitly_typed(const struct GC_calloc_typed_descr_s* p_ctd, size_t sizeof_ctd);
functions.description: Performs the actual allocation of a typed array using a descriptor previously prepared by GC_calloc_prepare_explicitly_typed. Intended for repeated allocations with the same element layout and array shape. The allocated memory corresponds to the parameters captured during preparation and is zero-initialized (inferred from calloc semantics).
requirements: p_ctd must point to a descriptor previously prepared by GC_calloc_prepare_explicitly_typed for the intended nelements/element_size_in_bytes and layout.
sizeof_ctd must equal sizeof(struct GC_calloc_typed_descr_s).
The prepared descriptor must still be valid at the time of the call (not corrupted or reclaimed).
Returned allocation is for the prepared array shape; contents are zeroed (inferred from the calloc family).

functions.name: GC_MALLOC_EXPLICITLY_TYPED
functions.description: Function-like macro that allocates a garbage-collected object whose pointer layout is described by descriptor d. In non-debug builds it maps to GC_malloc_explicitly_typed(bytes, d); in GC_DEBUG builds it ignores d and maps to GC_MALLOC(bytes). The returned object is cleared. Intended for performance-critical code needing precise pointer layout to reduce conservatism/leakage. The object must not be resized with GC_realloc/GC_reallocf.
requirements: bytes must be at least (number of meaningful bits in the bitmap of d) * sizeof(void*).
d should be a valid descriptor produced by GC_make_descriptor for the allocated object’s layout.
The returned object is cleared (zero-initialized).
The returned object must not be passed to GC_realloc() or GC_reallocf().
If GC_DEBUG is defined, d is ignored and the call is equivalent to GC_MALLOC(bytes).

functions.name: GC_MALLOC_EXPLICITLY_TYPED_IGNORE_OFF_PAGE
functions.description: Function-like macro variant of GC_MALLOC_EXPLICITLY_TYPED that, in non-debug builds, maps to GC_malloc_explicitly_typed_ignore_off_page(bytes, d) (which allocates using the descriptor while ignoring off-page references); in GC_DEBUG builds it ignores d and maps to GC_MALLOC(bytes). The returned object is cleared and must not be resized with GC_realloc/GC_reallocf.
requirements: bytes must be at least (number of meaningful bits in the bitmap of d) * sizeof(void*).
d should be a valid descriptor produced by GC_make_descriptor for the allocated object’s layout.
The returned object is cleared (zero-initialized).
The returned object must not be passed to GC_realloc() or GC_reallocf().
If GC_DEBUG is defined, d is ignored and the call is equivalent to GC_MALLOC(bytes).

functions.name: GC_CALLOC_EXPLICITLY_TYPED
functions.signature: void *GC_CALLOC_EXPLICITLY_TYPED(size_t nelements, size_t element_size_in_bytes, GC_descr d);
functions.description: Function-like macro that allocates an array of nelements elements, each of size element_size_in_bytes, with the element layout described by descriptor d. In non-debug builds it maps to GC_calloc_explicitly_typed(nelements, element_size_in_bytes, d); in GC_DEBUG builds it ignores d and maps to GC_MALLOC(nelements * element_size_in_bytes). The resulting memory is cleared.
requirements: element_size_in_bytes must be a multiple of the platform’s pointer alignment requirement.
element_size_in_bytes must be at least (number of meaningful bits in the bitmap of d) * sizeof(void*).
d should be a valid descriptor produced by GC_make_descriptor for the element layout.
The returned object is cleared (zero-initialized).
If GC_DEBUG is defined, d is ignored and the call is equivalent to GC_MALLOC(nelements * element_size_in_bytes).

functions.name: GC_init_finalized_malloc
functions.description: Initializes the dedicated object kind and disclaim machinery used by GC_finalized_malloc. Call from program/library initialization, and strictly before any finalized allocations via GC_finalized_malloc. The function is documented as thread-safe.
requirements: Must be called before any call to GC_finalized_malloc.
May be called during program/library initialization; function is thread-safe.
Only available when the library is built with ENABLE_DISCLAIM (API may be unavailable otherwise).

functions.name: GC_register_disclaim_proc
functions.signature: GC_API void GC_CALL GC_register_disclaim_proc(int kind, GC_disclaim_proc proc, int mark_from_all);
functions.description: Registers a disclaim callback proc for objects of the specified collector kind so it is invoked for each such object that becomes ready to be reclaimed. If proc returns nonzero, reclamation of that object is deferred for the current collection cycle. When mark_from_all is nonzero, any objects reachable from proc (including the closure object) are protected from collection, which may delay reclamation of long chains. Registration acquires the allocator lock; the callback is invoked with the allocator lock held. In find-leak mode this is a no-op.
requirements: proc must be a valid function pointer of type int (*)(void*); it will be called with the allocator lock held.
proc should not attempt to resurrect the object; returning nonzero merely defers reclamation for the current cycle.
kind must designate a valid GC object kind (exact range/meaning is library-specific and unknown from this header).
If mark_from_all is nonzero, the system will mark from all objects reachable from proc; callers should be aware this can delay collection of long reference chains.
Any call to GC_free for an object bypasses the disclaim callback and immediately deallocates that object.
Only effective when the library is built with ENABLE_DISCLAIM; in find-leak mode the registration is a no-op.

functions.name: GC_finalized_malloc
functions.signature: GC_API GC_ATTR_MALLOC GC_ATTR_ALLOC_SIZE(1) void *GC_CALL GC_finalized_malloc(size_t size, const struct GC_finalizer_closure *fc) GC_ATTR_NONNULL(2);
functions.description: Allocates a heap object that will be finalized using the provided finalizer closure fc and then reclaimed in the same collection cycle. This uses a dedicated object kind with a disclaim procedure and is more efficient than GC_register_finalizer APIs. Objects reachable from the finalizer (including a heap-allocated closure) are protected from collection during finalization. Note: GC_size on such an object may report slightly more than size, and GC_base returns a pointer to a word-sized header before the object start. The disclaim procedure is not invoked in find-leak mode; no debugging variant exists.
requirements: GC_init_finalized_malloc must be successfully called before using this function.
fc must be non-NULL and point to a valid GC_finalizer_closure with a callable GC_finalization_proc and associated client data.
The finalizer proc (fc->proc) should not attempt to resurrect the target object; the collector reclaims the object in the same cycle.
size is the requested allocation size in bytes (must fit in size_t).
Only available when the library is built with ENABLE_DISCLAIM (API may be unavailable otherwise).

functions.name: GC_get_back_ptr_info
functions.signature: GC_API GC_ref_kind GC_CALL GC_get_back_ptr_info(void *dest, void **base_p, size_t *offset_p) GC_ATTR_NONNULL(1);
functions.description: Returns information about what references the object containing dest. On success, writes the referring base address and offset to base_p and offset_p. If the referrer is a root, base_p will contain the root address and offset_p will be 0; if the referrer is a heap object, base_p will be non-NULL and offset_p will contain the offset within that object. If multiple referrers exist, the one most recently used by the collector to trace the object is reported. Intended for profiling/debugging; accuracy is not guaranteed for production use. Results are typically useful only immediately after a full GC (call GC_gcollect first).
requirements: dest must be non-NULL (GC_ATTR_NONNULL(1)).
dest should be an address within a heap object to obtain meaningful results; arbitrary addresses may yield GC_UNREFERENCED or GC_NO_SPACE.
If base_p is non-NULL, it must point to writable storage for a void* result.
If offset_p is non-NULL, it must point to writable storage for a size_t result.
Information is typically meaningful only after forcing a full garbage collection (call GC_gcollect() beforehand).
The allocator lock is not acquired by this function; it is intended for debugging/profiling, not production code.

functions.name: GC_generate_random_heap_address
functions.description: Returns a random address within the managed heap. The address is not guaranteed to fall within a valid object. Useful for debugging tools that probe heap structure or generate random backtraces.
requirements: Caller should hold the allocator lock while calling this function, as documented.
The returned address may not be inside a valid object; callers must validate before dereferencing or interpreting it.

functions.name: GC_generate_random_valid_address
functions.description: Returns a random address inside a valid, marked heap object. Useful for debugging/profiling scenarios that need a valid object interior pointer.
requirements: Caller should hold the allocator lock while calling this function, as documented.
Although the returned address is inside a valid marked object, callers must still avoid unsafe dereferences and respect object layout.

functions.name: GC_generate_random_backtrace
functions.description: Forces a garbage collection and emits a backtrace starting from a randomly chosen heap address using the collector’s logging (GC_printf). Often callable from a debugger to investigate retention paths.
requirements: This function triggers a garbage collection internally; callers should be prepared for GC side effects (e.g., finalization).
Output is produced via the collector logging mechanism (GC_printf); ensure logging is configured to observe results.

functions.name: GC_print_backtrace
functions.description: Prints a backtrace for a specific address using the collector’s logging. The client should force a full GC immediately before calling to ensure up-to-date reference info. Used internally by GC_generate_random_backtrace.
requirements: addr must be non-NULL (GC_ATTR_NONNULL(1)).
Caller should invoke GC_gcollect() immediately before calling this function to produce useful/accurate results.
The function outputs via GC_printf; ensure logging is enabled to see the backtrace.

functions.name: GC_init_gcj_malloc
functions.description: Initializes the GCJ-style allocation support in the Boehm GC. Must be called before any GC_gcj_* allocation functions are used. mp_index identifies a reserved mark-procedure slot and mp is a pointer to the mark procedure (type GC_mark_proc as defined in gc_mark.h). The mark procedure is used to build and apply descriptors for objects allocated through the GCJ debug interface (invoked with env==1) and may also be used by client-generated descriptors with a different env value. Deprecated in favor of GC_init_gcj_malloc_mp() for portable clients.
requirements: Must be called before any calls to GC_gcj_malloc, GC_debug_gcj_malloc, or GC_gcj_malloc_ignore_off_page.
mp_index must refer to a reserved mark procedure index that does not collide with indices allocated by GC_new_proc(); typically less than RESERVED_MARK_PROCS (e.g., GC_GCJ_RESERVED_MARK_PROC_INDEX).
mp must be a valid pointer to a function compatible with GC_mark_proc as defined in gc_mark.h; the collector will invoke it on debug-allocated objects with env==1.
If using client-generated mark descriptors that also reference mp, use a different env value to distinguish presence/absence of the debug header.
This API is deprecated; portable clients should prefer GC_init_gcj_malloc_mp() (requires including gc_mark.h).

functions.name: GC_gcj_malloc
functions.signature: void * GC_gcj_malloc(size_t lb, const void * vtable_ptr);
functions.description: Allocates a GCJ-style heap object of lb bytes, clears it to zero, and stores vtable_ptr as the first pointer-sized word in the object (the object’s type descriptor). Semantics mirror GC_malloc for size and clearing; if GC_malloc would add a trailing byte, this call does as well. On out-of-memory, GC_oom_fn() is invoked and its result is returned.
requirements: GC_init_gcj_malloc (or GC_init_gcj_malloc_mp) must have been called before using this allocator.
lb is the requested size in bytes and should be large enough to contain at least one pointer-sized word for the vtable pointer.

vtable_ptr should be a valid pointer to the object’s type descriptor ("vtable"); that descriptor is expected to contain a GC mark descriptor at offset GC_GCJ_MARK_DESCR_OFFSET, unless marking is provided via the registered mark procedure.
Callers must handle the possibility that the return value is NULL if GC_oom_fn() returns NULL or that the process may terminate depending on GC_oom_fn() behavior.
The vtable layout must satisfy that GC_GCJ_MARK_DESCR_OFFSET is not smaller than sizeof(void*), as assumed by the collector.

functions.name: GC_debug_gcj_malloc
functions.signature: void * GC_debug_gcj_malloc(size_t lb, const void * vtable_ptr, GC_EXTRA_PARAMS);
functions.description: Debug variant of GC_gcj_malloc. Allocates and zeroes a GCJ-style object of lb bytes, stores vtable_ptr as the first pointer-sized word, and attaches debug information. Objects allocated with this function are of kind GC_gcj_debug_kind.
requirements: GC_init_gcj_malloc (or GC_init_gcj_malloc_mp) must have been called before using this allocator.
lb is the size in bytes and should be large enough to hold at least a pointer-sized vtable field.

vtable_ptr should be a valid pointer to the object’s type descriptor that matches the collector’s expectations (mark descriptor available at GC_GCJ_MARK_DESCR_OFFSET or via the configured mark procedure).
GC_EXTRA_PARAMS must be supplied as defined by the build (typically debug metadata such as file/line); callers must pass arguments matching that macro’s signature.
Callers must handle the possibility of NULL return depending on GC_oom_fn() behavior.
Allocated objects belong to the GC_gcj_debug_kind kind; any code assuming a particular kind should use this fact only for debugging support.

functions.name: GC_gcj_malloc_ignore_off_page
functions.signature: void * GC_gcj_malloc_ignore_off_page(size_t lb, const void * vtable_ptr);
functions.description: Allocates and zeroes a GCJ-style object like GC_gcj_malloc, but optimized under the assumption that a pointer into the beginning of the object (within the first heap block) is always maintained while the object is live. This can reduce conservatism when scanning off-page interior pointers.
requirements: GC_init_gcj_malloc (or GC_init_gcj_malloc_mp) must have been called before using this allocator.

Use this function only if the program maintains at least one pointer to near the beginning of the object (within the first heap block) for the entire lifetime of the object; do not rely solely on interior pointers beyond the first block to keep the object alive.
lb is the size in bytes and should be sufficient to contain the vtable pointer as the first word.
vtable_ptr should be a valid pointer to the object’s type descriptor consistent with the collector’s expectations (mark descriptor at GC_GCJ_MARK_DESCR_OFFSET or compatible mark procedure).
Callers must handle possible NULL return depending on GC_oom_fn() behavior.

functions.name: GC_dlopen
functions.description: GC-aware replacement for dlopen. Allows the Boehm-Demers-Weiser GC to track dynamically loaded libraries so roots can be scanned correctly. Normally mapped to dlopen via macro redirection when GC_PTHREADS and redirection are enabled. Usage mirrors dlopen: pass a path and mode flags, receive a handle on success or NULL on failure.
requirements: Availability is conditional: only declared/redirected when GC_PTHREADS is defined and GC_NO_DLOPEN is not defined.
Arguments must satisfy dlopen semantics: the path may be NULL or a valid C string; mode must be a combination of platform-specific RTLD_* flags.
Caller must handle errors as with dlopen (e.g., check for NULL and use dlerror).
The returned handle must be closed with dlclose when no longer needed.

functions.name: GC_pthread_sigmask
functions.signature: GC_API int GC_pthread_sigmask(int, const sigset_t *, sigset_t *);
functions.description: GC-aware replacement for pthread_sigmask. Ensures the collector’s thread interception remains correct when threads change their signal masks. Mirrors pthread_sigmask usage: set or examine calling thread’s signal mask.
requirements: Availability is conditional: only declared when pthread_sigmask is available on the platform and GC_NO_PTHREAD_SIGMASK is not defined (various feature-test macros may enable it).
The 'how' argument must be one of SIG_BLOCK, SIG_UNBLOCK, or SIG_SETMASK.
'set' may be NULL to avoid changing the mask; if non-NULL, it must point to a valid sigset_t.
'oldset' may be NULL; if non-NULL, it must point to writable storage for the previous mask.
Return value semantics follow pthread_sigmask: 0 on success; otherwise an error number is returned.

functions.name: GC_pthread_create
functions.signature: GC_API int GC_pthread_create(pthread_t *, GC_PTHREAD_CREATE_CONST pthread_attr_t *, void *(*)(void *), void *);
functions.description: GC-aware replacement for pthread_create. Intercepts thread creation so the collector can register and scan thread stacks and coordinate stop-the-world. Intended to be transparently invoked via macro redirection of pthread_create.
requirements: Availability is conditional: declared when GC_PTHREADS is defined; macro redirection may be disabled via GC_NO_THREAD_REDIRECTS or GC_USE_LD_WRAP.
The first argument must be a non-NULL pointer to pthread_t storage to receive the new thread ID.
The 'attr' argument may be NULL or point to a valid pthread_attr_t with any settings acceptable to pthread_create.
The 'start_routine' must be a valid function pointer of type void *(*)(void *).
The 'arg' may be NULL or any pointer value passed to the start routine.
Return value semantics follow pthread_create: 0 on success; on error, a non-zero error number is returned, and no thread is created.

functions.name: GC_pthread_join
functions.description: GC-aware replacement for pthread_join. Ensures the collector coordinates properly when waiting for a thread to terminate. Mirrors pthread_join usage: join a joinable thread and optionally retrieve its exit value.
requirements: Availability is conditional: declared when GC_PTHREADS is defined; may be macro-redirected from pthread_join unless redirection is disabled.
The target pthread_t must refer to a valid, joinable thread that was not already joined and was not detached.
The 'retval' argument may be NULL or a pointer to receive the thread’s exit value.
Return value semantics follow pthread_join: 0 on success; otherwise an error number is returned.

functions.name: GC_pthread_detach
functions.description: GC-aware replacement for pthread_detach. Notifies the GC of detachment so it can manage thread lifecycle correctly. Usage mirrors pthread_detach: mark a joinable thread as detached.
requirements: Availability is conditional: declared when GC_PTHREADS is defined; may be macro-redirected from pthread_detach unless redirection is disabled.
The pthread_t must refer to a valid thread that is currently joinable (not already detached or joined).
Return value semantics follow pthread_detach: 0 on success; otherwise an error number is returned.

functions.name: GC_pthread_cancel
functions.description: GC-aware replacement for pthread_cancel. Intercepts cancellation requests so the collector maintains correct thread bookkeeping. Mirrors pthread_cancel usage: request that a thread be canceled.
requirements: Availability is conditional: only declared when GC_NO_PTHREAD_CANCEL is not defined and GC_PTHREADS is defined; may be macro-redirected from pthread_cancel unless disabled.
The pthread_t must refer to a valid thread.
Return value semantics follow pthread_cancel: 0 on success; otherwise an error number is returned.
Actual cancellation delivery depends on the target thread’s cancellation state and type.

functions.name: GC_pthread_exit
functions.description: GC-aware replacement for pthread_exit. Ensures the collector updates thread registration on thread termination. Mirrors pthread_exit usage: terminate the calling thread and make the value available to joiners. May carry an attribute via GC_PTHREAD_EXIT_ATTRIBUTE (e.g., noreturn).
requirements: Availability is conditional: only declared when GC_HAVE_PTHREAD_EXIT is defined (and not previously declared).
This function does not return; callers should not expect control to continue past the call.
The argument is the thread’s exit value; it may be NULL or any pointer value and can be retrieved by a joining thread.
Resources are released per pthread_exit semantics; thread-specific destructors may run.

functions.name: GC_MALLOC
functions.description: Allocates a garbage-collected heap block of at least size bytes and returns a pointer to it. Memory is traced by the Boehm GC and will be reclaimed automatically when unreachable. Use like malloc for GC-managed allocations.
requirements: size is the number of bytes to allocate; must be a non-negative value representable by size_t
Returned pointer should be treated as void* and cast to the desired type by the caller
The object should not be passed to non-GC deallocators; free with GC_FREE/free if explicit freeing is desired

functions.name: GC_FREE
functions.description: Explicitly frees a heap block previously allocated by a GC allocation routine (e.g., GC_MALLOC). In leak-detector/debug mode this records deallocation info. Normally unnecessary with conservative GC, but provided for compatibility and early reclamation.
requirements: ptr must be either NULL or a pointer previously returned by a GC allocator (e.g., GC_MALLOC/GC_REALLOC/GC_memalign/etc.)
Do not pass pointers not allocated by the GC; behavior is unspecified
May be called at most once per allocated object (double-free is invalid)

functions.name: GC_REALLOC
functions.description: Resizes a GC-managed allocation to size bytes. Semantics are analogous to C realloc but for GC-managed blocks; the returned pointer may differ from ptr.
requirements: ptr may be NULL (equivalent to GC_MALLOC) or must be a pointer returned by a GC allocator
size is the requested size in bytes; must be representable by size_t
On success, the old pointer value should not be used; use the returned pointer instead

functions.name: GC_REALLOCF
functions.description: BSD-like reallocf variant for GC-managed memory: attempts to resize ptr to size bytes; on failure it frees ptr and returns NULL. Use when you prefer automatic free on allocation failure.
requirements: ptr may be NULL or must be a pointer returned by a GC allocator
size is the requested size in bytes; must be representable by size_t
On allocation failure, the input ptr is freed and must not be used afterward

functions.name: GC_STRDUP
functions.description: Duplicates a NUL-terminated C string into a new GC-managed buffer and returns it. Acts like strdup but allocated memory is managed by the GC.
requirements: s must point to a valid NUL-terminated string
Returned string is GC-managed; do not free with non-GC deallocators; use GC_FREE/free if explicitly freeing

functions.name: GC_STRNDUP
functions.description: Duplicates at most n bytes from s, NUL-terminating the result, into a new GC-managed buffer. Acts like strndup but allocated memory is GC-managed.
requirements: s must point to a valid memory buffer; if not NUL-terminated within the first n bytes, only n bytes are copied and the result is NUL-terminated
n is the maximum number of bytes to copy
Returned string is GC-managed; use GC_FREE/free for explicit deallocation if desired

functions.name: GC_WCSDUP
functions.description: Duplicates a wide-character NUL-terminated string into a new GC-managed buffer, analogous to wcsdup. Mapping from wcsdup to this function occurs only if GC_REQUIRE_WCSDUP is defined and supported in the build.
requirements: s must point to a valid wide-character NUL-terminated string
Availability/macro redirection requires building the collector with GC_REQUIRE_WCSDUP defined (per header note)
Returned string is GC-managed; use GC_FREE/free for explicit deallocation if desired

functions.name: GC_FREEZERO
functions.description: Zeros n bytes of the allocation pointed to by ptr, then frees the object using the GC. Modeled after freezero available on some platforms.
requirements: ptr must be NULL or a pointer to a GC-allocated object
n should not exceed the size of the allocated object; otherwise behavior is unspecified
Call at most once per allocated object (double-free is invalid)

functions.name: GC_FREEZEROALL
functions.description: Zeros the entire allocation referenced by ptr, then frees it using the GC. Modeled after freezeroall present on some systems.
requirements: ptr must be NULL or a pointer to a GC-allocated object
Call at most once per allocated object (double-free is invalid)

functions.name: GC_memalign
functions.description: Allocates a GC-managed block of size bytes with a specified alignment. Acts like memalign/aligned_alloc but returns GC-managed memory. The header notes these aligned-allocation routines have no debugging counterparts; freeing may warn about missing debug info.
requirements: alignment should be a power of two and a multiple of sizeof(void*) (memalign/aligned_alloc conventions)
size is the number of bytes to allocate; must be representable by size_t
Free with GC_free/free; the debug/leak-detector may warn that the pointer has no debugging info

functions.name: GC_posix_memalign
functions.signature: int GC_posix_memalign(void **memptr, size_t alignment, size_t size);
functions.description: POSIX-style aligned allocation for GC-managed memory. On success stores a pointer to an aligned block of size bytes in *memptr and returns 0; on error returns an error code and leaves *memptr unspecified. The allocation is managed by the GC. The header notes aligned allocations may lack debugging info, causing warnings on free.
requirements: memptr must be a non-NULL pointer to a void* variable
alignment must be a power of two and a multiple of sizeof(void*) per POSIX
size is the number of bytes to allocate; must be representable by size_t
On success, the returned pointer should be freed with GC_free/free if explicit freeing is desired; debug/leak-detector may warn about missing debug info

functions.name: GC_free
functions.description: Frees a GC-managed block without recording debug information (non-debug free). Used internally by some macros and when debug info is not desired.
requirements: ptr must be NULL or a pointer previously allocated by a GC allocator
Do not call more than once for the same allocation (no double-free)

functions.name: GC_valloc
functions.description: Allocates a GC-managed block of size bytes aligned to a page boundary (like valloc). Intended for page-aligned allocations. The header notes aligned allocations lack debugging counterparts and may trigger warnings on free.
requirements: size is the number of bytes to allocate; must be representable by size_t
Free with GC_free/free if explicit freeing is desired; a warning about missing debug info may be emitted in debug/leak-detect mode

functions.name: GC_pvalloc
functions.description: Allocates a GC-managed block whose size is rounded up to a multiple of the page size and aligned to a page boundary (like pvalloc; considered obsolete). The header notes aligned allocations lack debugging counterparts and may trigger warnings on free.
requirements: size is the requested size in bytes; must be representable by size_t
Free with GC_free/free if explicit freeing is desired; a warning about missing debug info may be emitted in debug/leak-detect mode

functions.name: GC_size
functions.description: Returns the usable size in bytes of the GC-managed block pointed to by ptr (analogous to malloc_usable_size/malloc_size).
requirements: ptr should be a pointer previously returned by a GC allocator; passing non-GC pointers yields unspecified results
The returned size may be greater than or equal to the originally requested size

functions.name: GC_gcollect
functions.description: Forces an immediate full garbage collection cycle. In leak-detection mode this is also called automatically at program exit; the CHECK_LEAKS() macro maps to this call.
requirements: May be called at any time to request a full GC cycle
Callers should be prepared for the operation to be expensive and potentially stop-the-world

functions.name: CORD_cat
functions.description: Concatenate two cords into a new cord. If either argument is a C string (direct char*-backed cord), that storage may be shared by the result and must not be modified after the call.
requirements: x and y may be NULL to represent empty cords.
If x or y are C strings, the caller must not modify the underlying char buffers after passing them to this function (they may be shared by the result).
The returned cord is immutable from the API perspective.

functions.name: CORD_cat_char_star
functions.signature: CORD CORD_cat_char_star(CORD x, const char *y, size_t y_len);
functions.description: Concatenate a cord with a C string of known length. Faster than CORD_cat when the length is known. The y buffer is shared with the resulting cord and must not be modified by the caller.
requirements: y points to at least y_len bytes of valid storage; it need not be NUL-terminated.
The caller must not modify the memory pointed to by y after the call, since it may be shared by the resulting cord.
x may be NULL to represent an empty cord.

functions.name: CORD_len
functions.description: Return the length (number of characters) of a cord.
requirements: x may be NULL to represent an empty cord.

functions.name: CORD_from_fn
functions.signature: CORD CORD_from_fn(CORD_fn f, void *client_data, size_t len);
functions.description: Create a cord whose characters are produced by a callback function f(i, client_data) for 0 <= i < len. Supports embedding NUL characters. Useful for lazily-defined or generated strings.
requirements: f must be a valid function pointer usable for indices 0..len-1.
f should be safe to call multiple times for the same i and may be called in arbitrary order; it should not rely on destructive side effects.
len specifies the cord length; f must return a char for each index in [0, len).
client_data is passed through unchanged to each callback invocation.

functions.name: CORD_substr
functions.signature: CORD CORD_substr(CORD x, size_t i, size_t n);
functions.description: Return a subcord of x starting at position i (0-based) with length at most n. The result is a view-like cord and typically shares structure with x.
requirements: 0-based index i refers to the first character to include; n caps the length of the returned subcord.
If i is past the end of x, the behavior is unspecified by this header; callers should ensure i <= CORD_len(x).

functions.name: CORD_balance
functions.description: Return a rebalanced version of x to improve performance of character access, substrings, and comparisons (e.g., after many concatenations). The argument is not modified; only the returned cord is balanced.
requirements: x may be any cord (possibly the result of many concatenations).
Callers should continue using the returned cord for improved asymptotic access; the function may reallocate significant internal structure.

functions.name: CORD_iter5
functions.signature: int CORD_iter5(CORD x, size_t i, CORD_iter_fn f1, CORD_batched_iter_fn f2, void *client_data);
functions.description: Iterate forward over characters of x starting at index i, calling f1 for each character. If f2 is not CORD_NO_FN, the implementation may batch contiguous substrings and call f2 instead. Iteration stops at string end or when a callback returns nonzero; the return value is nonzero if a callback aborted the traversal, 0 otherwise.
requirements: i must be less than CORD_len(x).
f1 must be a valid function pointer; it is called as f1(char, client_data).
f2 may be CORD_NO_FN; if provided, it must accept a NUL-terminated C substring pointer and client_data. The substring is read-only and valid only during the call.
Callbacks must return 0 to continue, nonzero to stop.

functions.name: CORD_riter4
functions.signature: int CORD_riter4(CORD x, size_t i, CORD_iter_fn f1, void *client_data);
functions.description: Iterate backward over characters of x starting at index i down to the beginning, calling f1 for each character. Stops at string start or when f1 returns nonzero; returns nonzero if aborted by the callback, 0 otherwise.
requirements: i must be less than CORD_len(x).
f1 must be a valid function pointer; it is called as f1(char, client_data).
Callback must return 0 to continue, nonzero to stop.

functions.name: CORD_riter
functions.signature: int CORD_riter(CORD x, CORD_iter_fn f1, void *client_data);
functions.description: Reverse-iterate over all characters of x starting from the end, calling f1 for each character. Returns nonzero if aborted by the callback, 0 otherwise.
requirements: f1 must be a valid function pointer; it is called as f1(char, client_data).
Callback must return 0 to continue, nonzero to stop.

functions.name: CORD_set_oom_fn
functions.description: Set the out-of-memory handler function used by the cords library. A NULL value means do nothing special (just abort).
requirements: fn may be NULL to request default abort-on-OOM behavior.
The handler must be async-signal-safe only if used in such contexts (not specified here); otherwise it should avoid undefined behavior.

functions.name: CORD_get_oom_fn
functions.description: Get the current out-of-memory handler function pointer used by the cords library.

functions.name: CORD_dump
functions.description: Dump an implementation-defined representation of x to stdout for debugging purposes.
requirements: For debugging only; output format is implementation-defined.

functions.name: CORD_cat_char
functions.description: Concatenate a single character c to the end of cord x and return the result.
requirements: x may be NULL to represent an empty cord.

functions.name: CORD_catn
functions.description: Concatenate n cords passed as variadic arguments and return the result.
requirements: n specifies the number of subsequent CORD arguments provided in the varargs; the caller must pass exactly n CORD arguments.
n should be nonnegative. Behavior for negative n is undefined.
Each provided argument must be a valid CORD (may be NULL for empty).

functions.name: CORD_fetch
functions.description: Return the character at index i of x (equivalent to CORD_substr(x, i, 1)).
requirements: Caller should ensure i < CORD_len(x). The header implies this via the substr equivalence but does not restate it explicitly.

functions.name: CORD_cmp
functions.description: Lexicographically compare two cords. Returns <0 if x<y, 0 if x==y, >0 if x>y.
requirements: x and y may be NULL to represent empty cords.

functions.name: CORD_ncmp
functions.signature: int CORD_ncmp(CORD x, size_t x_start, CORD y, size_t y_start, size_t len);
functions.description: Lexicographically compare up to len characters of subcords starting at x_start in x and y_start in y. Returns <0, 0, or >0 similar to strncmp semantics.
requirements: x_start and y_start are 0-based start indices into their respective cords.

Comparison stops after len characters or when either subcord ends, whichever comes first. Exact handling of out-of-range starts is not specified in the header; callers should use values within the cord lengths.

functions.name: CORD_str
functions.signature: size_t CORD_str(CORD x, size_t start, CORD s);
functions.description: Find the first occurrence of subcord s in x at or after position start. Returns the index of the first matching character, or CORD_NOT_FOUND if no match is found.
requirements: start must be less than or equal to CORD_len(x); the comment specifies positions at or later than start and implies valid indexing.
s may be NULL to represent an empty cord; the behavior in that case is not specified here.

functions.name: CORD_chars
functions.description: Create a cord consisting of i copies of the character c. The representation uses space independent of i (constant space). May embed NUL characters.
requirements: i is the requested length (0 allowed).
When combined with CORD_to_char_star, embedded NULs in the result may lead to shorter C strings if interpreted via strlen; callers should be aware of this.

functions.name: CORD_from_file
functions.description: Create a cord representing the contents of file f. Short files may be read immediately; long files may be read on demand. The implementation may access f immediately and later as the cord is used; it arranges to close f when it is no longer needed.
requirements: f must be a seekable stream whose contents remain constant for the life of the cord.
The library must have exclusive access to f: it may read at any time and assumes the file position remains where it left it.
ftell(f) must reflect the actual character position (number of bytes readable by fread). On Windows, f must be opened in binary mode.
Caller typically invokes as CORD_from_file(fopen(...)). Do not use f after passing it to this function, as the library manages and eventually closes it.

functions.name: CORD_from_file_eager
functions.description: Create a cord from file f by reading the entire file content immediately; the file is closed immediately after reading. The binary-mode restriction does not apply for this eager variant.
requirements: f must be a valid readable FILE*.
After the call, the caller must not use f, as it will be closed by the function.

functions.name: CORD_from_file_lazy
functions.description: Create a cord from file f that reads content on demand (lazy). The binary-mode restriction applies on Windows.
requirements: f must be seekable and readable, with contents remaining constant.
On Windows, f must be opened in binary mode.
The library requires exclusive access to f and may read it later; do not read from or reposition f in user code after passing it.

functions.name: CORD_to_char_star
functions.description: Convert a cord to a newly-allocated, modifiable C string with no shared structure with the source cord. Embedded NULs in x remain in the result buffer.
requirements: x may contain embedded NULs; the returned C string may contain NUL bytes within its length.
Ownership/allocator of the returned buffer is not specified in this header; caller responsibilities for freeing are unknown.

functions.name: CORD_from_char_star
functions.description: Create a cord by copying a NUL-terminated C string s, so the original s may be modified later without affecting the cord.
requirements: s must point to a valid NUL-terminated C string.

functions.name: CORD_to_const_char_star
functions.description: Create a const char* representation of x that may share structure with the original cord. The result must be treated as read-only and not modified.
requirements: The returned pointer may alias internal storage; the caller must not write through it.
Lifetime/validity of the returned pointer is not specified here; callers should avoid retaining it beyond typical use without holding on to x.

functions.name: CORD_put
functions.description: Write a cord to a FILE stream starting at the current file position. No trailing NUL or newline is added. Returns EOF on write error, 1 on success.
requirements: f must be a valid writable FILE*.
x may contain embedded NULs; the function writes the actual bytes.

functions.name: CORD_chr
functions.signature: size_t CORD_chr(CORD x, size_t i, int c);
functions.description: Return the index of the first occurrence of character c in x at or after position i. Returns CORD_NOT_FOUND if not present.
requirements: i must be less than CORD_len(x).
c is interpreted as an unsigned char value promoted to int (as with standard strchr-like behavior).

functions.name: CORD_rchr
functions.signature: size_t CORD_rchr(CORD x, size_t i, int c);
functions.description: Return the index of the last occurrence of character c in x at or before position i. Returns CORD_NOT_FOUND if not present.
requirements: i must be less than CORD_len(x).
c is interpreted as an unsigned char value promoted to int.

functions.name: CORD_sprintf
functions.description: Format data according to a CORD format string and assign the resulting cord to *out. Supports %r to format a CORD argument (with width/precision like %s). The format string itself is copied; CORD arguments included via %r are not copied and may share structure with the result. Returns the number of characters produced, or -1 on error.
requirements: out must be a valid pointer to a CORD variable; the function assigns through it.
format must be a valid CORD containing a printf-style format string; use %r to pass a CORD argument.
Variadic arguments must match the format specifiers exactly (including using CORD for %r).

functions.name: CORD_vsprintf
functions.signature: int CORD_vsprintf(CORD *out, CORD format, va_list args);
functions.description: va_list variant of CORD_sprintf. Formats according to a CORD format string and assigns the result to *out. %r formats a CORD. Returns the number of characters produced, or -1 on error.
requirements: out must be a valid pointer to a CORD variable.
format must be a valid CORD containing a printf-style format string with any %r expecting a CORD.
args must be an initialized va_list corresponding to the format string and must remain valid for the duration of the call.

functions.name: CORD_fprintf
functions.description: Like fprintf but with the format string as a CORD and support for %r to format a CORD. Writes to stream. Returns the number of characters produced, or -1 on error.
requirements: stream must be a valid writable FILE*.
Variadic arguments must match the format string, using CORD for any %r.

functions.name: CORD_vfprintf
functions.signature: int CORD_vfprintf(FILE *stream, CORD format, va_list args);
functions.description: va_list variant of CORD_fprintf. Formats using a CORD format string (supports %r for cords) and writes to stream. Returns the number of characters produced, or -1 on error.
requirements: stream must be a valid writable FILE*.
args must be an initialized va_list matching the format string and remain valid during the call.

functions.name: CORD_printf
functions.description: Like printf to stdout but with the format string as a CORD and support for %r to format a CORD. Returns the number of characters produced, or -1 on error.
requirements: Variadic arguments must match the format string, using CORD for any %r.

functions.name: CORD_vprintf
functions.description: va_list variant of CORD_printf using a CORD format string (supports %r for cords) and writing to stdout. Returns the number of characters produced, or -1 on error.
requirements: args must be an initialized va_list matching the format string and remain valid during the call.

functions.name: CORD_pos_to_cord
functions.description: Extracts the cord object associated with a CORD position. In this header, the public name is a macro that returns p[0].path[0].pe_cord directly. Use to recover the underlying cord from an existing position.
requirements: p must be a valid CORD_pos object (an array of length 1) previously initialized (e.g., via CORD_set_pos or equivalent).
No guarantee is stated about behavior if the position is invalid; returned cord is whatever is stored in p[0].path[0].pe_cord.

functions.name: CORD_pos_to_index
functions.description: Returns the current character index within the cord for the given position. In this header, the public name is a macro that returns p[0].cur_pos.
requirements: p must be a valid CORD_pos object (array of length 1) previously initialized.
If the position is invalid, the returned index may not refer to a valid character; no explicit guarantees are provided.

functions.name: CORD_pos_fetch
functions.description: Fetches the character at the current position. Implemented as a macro that returns from a cached leaf if available, otherwise calls the slow-path CORD__pos_fetch(p).
requirements: p must be initialized.
p should be valid (inside the cord) for meaningful results; behavior when invalid is not specified in this header.
If the cache is unavailable (p[0].cur_end == 0), the function calls CORD__pos_fetch(p) to obtain the character.

functions.name: CORD_set_pos
functions.signature: void CORD_set_pos(CORD_pos p, CORD c, size_t index);
functions.description: Initializes a position to refer to the given cord c at the specified index. This is noted as the most expensive position operation; typically used to begin iteration at an arbitrary index.
requirements: p must be a CORD_pos object (array of length 1).
c must be a valid CORD object.

index should designate the target character position within c. The valid range is not explicitly stated; callers should ensure index is within the cord length to obtain a valid position. Behavior for out-of-range indices is unspecified (the position may be invalidated).

functions.name: CORD_next
functions.description: Advances the position to the next character. Implemented as a macro that increments within the cached range or calls CORD__next(p) when crossing a cache boundary. Invalidates the position if it advances past the end of the cord.
requirements: p must be initialized and valid before the call.
If the advancement would move past the end of the cord, the position becomes invalid.
Callers should check CORD_pos_valid(p) after advancing if end-of-cord is possible.

functions.name: CORD_prev
functions.description: Moves the position to the previous character. Implemented as a macro that decrements within the cached range or calls CORD__prev(p) when crossing a cache boundary. Invalidates the position if it moves past the beginning of the cord.
requirements: p must be initialized and valid before the call.
If the movement would go before the beginning of the cord, the position becomes invalid.
Callers should check CORD_pos_valid(p) after moving if beginning-of-cord is possible.

functions.name: CORD_pos_valid
functions.description: Returns non-zero if the position is currently valid (i.e., refers to a character inside the cord). Implemented as a macro that tests p[0].path_len against CORD_POS_INVALID.
requirements: p must be a CORD_pos object (array of length 1).
No other preconditions are documented.

functions.name: CORD__pos_fetch
functions.description: Slow-path helper used by the CORD_pos_fetch macro to fetch the character at the current position when the fast cache is not available. Intended for internal use and performance-critical paths; behavior should mirror CORD_pos_fetch.
requirements: p must be initialized.
p should be valid (inside the cord) for meaningful results; behavior when invalid is not specified in this header.

functions.name: CORD__next
functions.description: Slow-path helper used by the CORD_next macro to advance the position when crossing cache boundaries or when no cached leaf is available. May invalidate the position if it advances past the end of the cord.
requirements: p must be initialized and valid before the call.
If advancement goes past the end, the position becomes invalid.
Typically not called directly by users; invoked via the CORD_next macro on slow paths.

functions.name: CORD__prev
functions.description: Slow-path helper used by the CORD_prev macro to move the position backward when crossing cache boundaries or when no cached leaf is available. May invalidate the position if it moves before the beginning of the cord.
requirements: p must be initialized and valid before the call.
If movement goes before the beginning, the position becomes invalid.
Typically not called directly by users; invoked via the CORD_prev macro on slow paths.

functions.name: CORD_ec_flush_buf
functions.description: Flushes the buffered characters in the extensible cord x into its underlying cord (x[0].ec_cord) and resets the buffer pointer. Typically invoked implicitly by the other macros when needed (e.g., when converting to a CORD or when the buffer fills), but can be called directly. Use after accumulating characters via CORD_ec_append and before observing the final CORD value.
requirements: x must refer to a valid, initialized extensible cord object created as: CORD_ec x; and initialized with CORD_ec_init(x).
Do not pass the address of an element; pass the CORD_ec array object itself (the type is an array of one struct and the API expects that exact type).
x must not be NULL; it is mutated in place.
The function is not documented as thread-safe; callers should not concurrently access the same CORD_ec from multiple threads.

functions.name: CORD_ec_to_cord
functions.description: Converts an extensible cord to a CORD by first flushing any buffered characters, then yielding the current accumulated cord value. Intended for retrieving the result after building up an extensible cord. The resulting CORD can be further processed (e.g., balanced or converted to a C string) as needed.
requirements: x must be a valid, initialized CORD_ec (declare as CORD_ec x; and initialize with CORD_ec_init(x)).
x is evaluated multiple times by the macro; do not pass an expression with side effects (use a simple lvalue like x).
After obtaining the CORD, consider calling CORD_balance or CORD_to_char_star if you need a balanced cord or a C string, respectively (usage guidance; not a strict requirement).

functions.name: CORD_ec_init
functions.description: Initializes an extensible cord object x by setting its underlying cord to empty and its buffer pointer to the start of the internal buffer. Call this before any append operations. Typical usage: declare CORD_ec x; then call CORD_ec_init(x) once before building the cord.
requirements: x must denote storage of type CORD_ec, typically declared as: CORD_ec x; (it is an array of one struct).
x is evaluated multiple times by the macro; pass a simple lvalue (no side effects).
Must be called before any use of x with CORD_ec_append, CORD_ec_append_cord, or CORD_ec_to_cord.
Reinitializing an in-use CORD_ec will reset its state; whether this is intended in a given context is up to the caller (behavior beyond resetting is not documented).

functions.name: CORD_ec_append
functions.description: Appends a single character c to the extensible cord x. Characters are buffered internally until the buffer fills (size CORD_BUFSZ), at which point the buffer is flushed into the underlying cord automatically.
requirements: x must be a valid, initialized CORD_ec (via CORD_ec_init(x)).
x is evaluated multiple times by the macro; pass a simple lvalue (no side effects).
c is assigned into a char buffer; it must be representable as a char (it will be converted to char).
No explicit flushing by the caller is needed for buffer-full conditions; the macro flushes automatically when the buffer reaches CORD_BUFSZ.

functions.name: CORD_ec_append_cord
functions.description: Appends the cord c to the extensible cord x. The resulting structure shares representation with c (no deep copy). Use this to concatenate an existing cord onto an extensible cord you are building. Any necessary coordination with x’s internal buffer is handled by the implementation.
requirements: x must be a valid, initialized extensible cord (declare as CORD_ec x; and initialize with CORD_ec_init(x)).
Do not pass the address of an element; pass the CORD_ec array object itself (matches the parameter type).
c must be a valid CORD value as defined by cord.h; sharing semantics mean c should remain valid for the lifetime of any structures that reference it.
The function mutates x; callers should not concurrently access the same CORD_ec from multiple threads.

functions.name: GC_finalize_all
functions.description: Invokes all remaining finalizers that have not yet been run. Intended for strict Java-style finalization compliance; not recommended for general use. It acquires the allocator lock and may run finalizers repeatedly until none remain. The notifier is not called, so it should be invoked from a separate thread. May block for an extended time if finalizers enqueue more finalizable objects.
requirements: Should be called from a separate thread (the notifier is not called).
Caller must tolerate that it may run for a long time or indefinitely if finalizers keep creating new finalizable objects.
Caller must tolerate that the allocator lock is acquired internally.

functions.name: GC_suspend_thread
functions.description: Externally suspends the specified thread for the garbage collector. There is no suspension count; a thread suspended multiple times will be resumed by the first call to GC_resume_thread(). It acquires the allocator lock. Functionality is unimplemented on some platforms and is not recommended for general use.
requirements: Available only when GC_THREADS is defined at compile time.
The thread identified by the GC_SUSPEND_THREAD_ID must be registered in the collector.
Do not assume nested or reference-counted suspension semantics; a single GC_resume_thread() may resume a thread even if GC_suspend_thread() was called multiple times.
Caller must tolerate that the allocator lock is acquired internally.
May be unimplemented on some platforms; caller must ensure platform support before relying on this behavior.

functions.name: GC_resume_thread
functions.description: Resumes a thread previously suspended via the collector’s external suspension mechanism. There is no suspension count; the very first call to GC_resume_thread() will resume a thread even if it has been suspended multiple times. It acquires the allocator lock. Not recommended for general use and unimplemented on some platforms.
requirements: Available only when GC_THREADS is defined at compile time.
The thread identified by the GC_SUSPEND_THREAD_ID should be registered in the collector.
Do not rely on nested suspension semantics; a single call may resume a thread that was suspended multiple times.
Caller must tolerate that the allocator lock is acquired internally.

import random
import string
from typing import List

# Target data type: NUL-terminated C string
# The fuzzer stubs call FUZZ_PARAM_STR() for inputs to strdup-like APIs and
# other const char* parameters. We therefore generate byte sequences that are
# valid C strings (ASCII/UTF-8 friendly), NUL-terminated, without embedded NULs
# in the significant portion, and with a variety of content to exercise paths:
# - empty strings
# - short/medium/long lengths
# - mixed character classes (printables, whitespace, punctuation)
# - edge-y constructs (very long single-char repeats, path-like strings,
#   format-like strings with % specifiers, Unicode UTF-8 sequences)
# The returned bytes buffer will be consumed by the harness to feed successive
# FUZZ_PARAM_STR() calls as substrings; typical fuzzers use the buffer and split
# internally. We thus concatenate multiple NUL-terminated strings to provide
# several distinct values in one buffer. This also covers the cases where the
# same buffer is reused for multiple API calls within a single stub invocation.

MAX_TOTAL = 4096

# Character pools
PRINTABLE = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + string.punctuation + " "
WHITESPACE = " \t\r\n\v\f"
PATH_CHARS = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + "._-/\\"
FORMAT_SPEC = ["%s", "%d", "%u", "%p", "%x", "%zu", "%%", "%08x", "%lld", "%.*s"]

# Some UTF-8 snippets (valid)
UTF8_SNIPPETS = [
    "π", "£", "你好", "🙂", "⌘", "über", "mañana", "русский", "العربية",
]


def _rand_choice(rng: random.Random, seq: List[str]):
    return seq[rng.randrange(len(seq))]


def _make_c_string(rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Choose a pattern to diversify strings
    kind = rng.randrange(10)
    if kind == 0:
        # Empty string
        s = ""
    elif kind == 1:
        # Short random printable
        n = rng.randint(1, 32)
        s = "".join(rng.choice(PRINTABLE) for _ in range(n))
    elif kind == 2:
        # Long random printable
        n = rng.randint(128, 1024)
        s = "".join(rng.choice(PRINTABLE) for _ in range(n))
    elif kind == 3:
        # Repeated single character
        ch = rng.choice(PRINTABLE)
        n = rng.randint(1, 1024)
        s = ch * n
    elif kind == 4:
        # Whitespace-heavy
        n = rng.randint(1, 128)
        s = "".join(rng.choice(WHITESPACE + PRINTABLE) for _ in range(n))
        # Ensure no embedded NULs (none from our pools)
    elif kind == 5:
        # File/path-like
        parts = ["/", "tmp", "var", "usr", "lib", "home", "data", "logs"]
        depth = rng.randint(1, 6)
        seg = lambda: "".join(rng.choice(PATH_CHARS) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 12)))
        s = "/".join([_rand_choice(rng, parts)] + [seg() for _ in range(depth)])
        if rng.random() < 0.3:
            s += "." + _rand_choice(rng, ["txt", "bin", "log", "dat", "json"]) 
    elif kind == 6:
        # Format-string-like
        n = rng.randint(1, 8)
        tokens = []
        for _ in range(n):
            if rng.random() < 0.5:
                tokens.append("".join(rng.choice(PRINTABLE) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 6))))
            tokens.append(_rand_choice(rng, FORMAT_SPEC))
        s = "_".join(tokens)
    elif kind == 7:
        # UTF-8 sequences mixed with ASCII
        base = "".join(rng.choice(PRINTABLE) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 16)))
        utf = _rand_choice(rng, UTF8_SNIPPETS)
        tail = "".join(rng.choice(PRINTABLE) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 16)))
        s = base + utf + tail
    elif kind == 8:
        # Numeric string
        if rng.random() < 0.5:
            s = str(rng.randrange(0, 1 << 32))
        else:
            s = hex(rng.randrange(0, 1 << 64))
    else:
        # Mixed chunks
        chunks = []
        for _ in range(rng.randint(2, 6)):
            subk = rng.randrange(6)
            if subk in (0, 1):
                chunks.append("".join(rng.choice(PRINTABLE) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 16))))
            elif subk == 2:
                chunks.append(_rand_choice(rng, FORMAT_SPEC))
            elif subk == 3:
                chunks.append(_rand_choice(rng, UTF8_SNIPPETS))
            elif subk == 4:
                chunks.append(str(rng.randrange(0, 100000)))
            else:
                chunks.append("/" + "".join(rng.choice(PATH_CHARS) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 8))))
        s = "".join(chunks)

    # Encode as UTF-8; ensure no embedded NUL; terminate with NUL
    b = s.encode('utf-8', errors='ignore')
    b = b.replace(b"\x00", b"")
    return b + b"\x00"


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    # Compose multiple C strings back-to-back to feed multiple FUZZ_PARAM_STR calls.
    # Include a variety of lengths and patterns while keeping under MAX_TOTAL.
    out = bytearray()

    # Always include corner cases first
    for fixed in [b"\x00", b"A\x00", b"hello world\x00", b"/tmp/test.txt\x00", b"%s_%08x\x00"]:
        if len(out) + len(fixed) > MAX_TOTAL:
            break
        out += fixed

    # Then add a random number of generated strings
    target = rng.randint(8, 24)
    for _ in range(target):
        s = _make_c_string(rng)
        if len(out) + len(s) > MAX_TOTAL:
            break
        out += s

    # Ensure buffer is non-empty and ends with a NUL-terminated string
    if not out:
        out += b"\x00"
    if out[-1] != 0:
        out += b"\x00"

    return bytes(out)

import os
import random
import struct
from typing import List

# Target: inputs feed FUZZ_PARAM_STR() for pointer-range APIs and string duplication.
# We want buffers that are:
# - Non-empty (so ranges [bottom, top) are valid)
# - Sometimes large, sometimes small
# - Contain interior NULs and varied bytes to exercise different n in STRNDUP
# - Have repeated patterns and random data so i/j subranges vary in content
# - Include aligned-looking regions to resemble pointers/address-like data
# - <= 4096 bytes

_MAX = 4096

def _rand(rng: random.Random, a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return rng.randint(a, b)

def _emit_pattern(rng: random.Random, length: int) -> bytes:
    chunks: List[bytes] = []

    # 1) Header with magic and lengths to create recognizable regions
    magic = rng.choice([b"GC\x00\x01", b"CORD\x00", b"\xDE\xAD\xBE\xEF", b"\xCA\xFE\xBA\xBE"]) 
    chunks.append(magic)

    # 2) A block of zeroes to create long NUL runs
    zlen = _rand(rng, 4, min(64, max(4, length // 16)))
    chunks.append(b"\x00" * zlen)

    # 3) Repeating short pattern to create interesting subranges
    patt = rng.choice([b"AB", b"\xFF\x00", b"xyZ", b"\x7F\x80\x81\x82"]) 
    reps = _rand(rng, 4, 64)
    chunks.append(patt * reps)

    # 4) Random bytes block
    rlen = _rand(rng, 16, max(16, length // 8))
    chunks.append(os.urandom(rlen))

    # 5) ASCII-ish segment with occasional NULs to test STRNDUP boundaries
    alen = _rand(rng, 16, 128)
    ascii_bytes = bytearray()
    for i in range(alen):
        if rng.random() < 0.08:
            ascii_bytes.append(0)
        else:
            ascii_bytes.append(rng.choice([32, 46, 47, 58, 65, 66, 67, 95, 97, 98, 99, 120, 121, 122]))
    chunks.append(bytes(ascii_bytes))

    # 6) Address-like words (little-endian) to resemble plausible pointers
    # Though not dereferenced, these can exercise valid/invalid displacement checks
    wcount = _rand(rng, 4, 32)
    words = bytearray()
    for _ in range(wcount):
        # Mix in low and high addresses
        val = rng.choice([
            rng.getrandbits(32),
            0,
            0xFFFFFFFF,
            0x1000 * _rand(rng, 1, 1024),
        ])
        words += struct.pack("<I", val)
    chunks.append(bytes(words))

    # 7) Another random slab
    chunks.append(os.urandom(_rand(rng, 8, 64)))

    blob = b"".join(chunks)
    if len(blob) >= length:
        return blob[:length]

    # 8) Fill remaining with a mix of patterned and random data
    remaining = length - len(blob)
    tail = bytearray()
    while remaining > 0:
        choice = rng.random()
        if choice < 0.3:
            # More zeroes
            seg = b"\x00" * min(remaining, _rand(rng, 1, 64))
        elif choice < 0.6:
            # Repeat previous pattern
            seg = patt * _rand(rng, 1, max(1, min(16, remaining // max(1, len(patt)))))
            seg = seg[:remaining]
        else:
            # Random block
            seg = os.urandom(min(remaining, _rand(rng, 8, 128)))
        tail += seg
        remaining -= len(seg)
    return blob + bytes(tail)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    # Size strategy: choose among small, medium, large while keeping <= 4096
    size_choice = rng.random()
    if size_choice < 0.2:
        length = _rand(rng, 1, 32)  # very small buffers
    elif size_choice < 0.7:
        length = _rand(rng, 64, 1024)  # common case
    else:
        length = _rand(rng, 1024, _MAX)  # large buffers to exercise wide ranges

    data = _emit_pattern(rng, length)

    # Ensure non-empty and bounded
    if not data:
        data = b"\x00"
    if len(data) > _MAX:
        data = data[:_MAX]
    return data
